AuthorAniket Pandey
Published byLayer One, Bangalore

Year2026

About this edition

A field guide for the people who decide whether a design system gets built, and how.

This playbook exists because most writing about design systems is either a vendor pitch or a component tutorial. Neither helps a founder decide whether to invest, a design leader plan the first year, or an engineering leader understand what they are signing up to maintain.

It is written by Aniket Pandey, who leads Layer One, a design systems studio in Bangalore. Aniket has built design systems at IBM (for clients including Cardinal Health and Riyadh Air), led the design system at CARS24 across 10+ products in three countries, and works on design system tooling and governance at JPMorgan Chase.1 The playbook distils that work, plus the published practice of the most mature public systems, into decisions you can act on.

How to read the evidence

Not every claim in this book is equally certain, and we think you should know which is which. Every claim that matters carries one of four labels:

Standard
A normative specification, such as WCAG 2.2. If you claim conformance, it is not optional.
Documented
Published research, a case study or official system documentation. Cited, with caveats where the sample is small or vendor-run.
Practice
Layer One's recommendation from practice. Reasoned and tested, but not universal. Disagree when your context differs.
Illustrative
A worked example with stated assumptions. It is not a measured result, so treat the method as the lesson, not the numbers.

We do not invent statistics, case studies or outcomes. Worked examples use Ledgerly, a fictional B2B finance product, so you never mistake an illustration for a client result. All colour values, contrast ratios and type scales in the figures are computed by the build script from the data files in the repository, not typed by hand.

Understanding design systems: does your company actually need one?

Before anyone opens Figma, five questions decide whether a design system succeeds: what it is, whether you need it now, what it is worth, what it costs, and who will run it. This part answers all five.

  1. 01What a design system actually is
  2. 02Who needs one, and when

Chapter 01

What a design system actually is

A design system is not a Figma file and it is not a component library. It is a shared agreement about how your product gets made, encoded in tools that design and engineering both use, and kept alive by people whose job it is to keep it alive.

Read this if

You have heard "design system" used for five different things in one meeting, or you need to explain to leadership what you are actually proposing to fund.

What you'll leave with
  1. A precise, defensible definition you can put in a strategy document.
  2. The ability to tell a style guide, UI kit, component library and design system apart, and to know which one you have today.
  3. A clear picture of why a system's value grows faster than the organisation using it.

01.1A working definition

The term is used loosely, and the looseness causes real damage. Leadership approves a "design system" thinking it bought consistency. The design team ships a Figma library. Engineering never adopts it. Eighteen months later the product still has nine kinds of button, and everyone concludes design systems don't work.

So we start with a definition precise enough to plan against:

Definition

A design system is the set of shared decisions, reusable assets and working agreements that lets many people build one coherent product, plus the team and process that keep all three current.

Each of the three parts matters, and most failed systems are missing one of them.

01 — Decisions

What we've agreed

Principles, foundations (colour, type, spacing, layout, motion), accessibility targets, content voice. The why behind every asset.

02 — Assets

What we've built

Design tokens, components in the design tool and in code, patterns, templates, icons and the documentation that explains them.

03 — Agreements

How we work

Ownership, contribution, review, versioning, release and deprecation. The rules for how the first two change over time.

Decisions without assets are a PDF nobody opens. Assets without decisions are a library that encodes whatever inconsistency already existed. Decisions and assets without agreements drift out of date within a year. Layer One's first working rule says it plainly:

A design system is an agreement, not a library.Rule #1 — Layer One

A short lineage

Organisations have codified visual decisions for decades, in brand manuals and corporate identity standards. What changed in software was that the decisions had to be executable. Pattern libraries spread through web teams in the early 2010s. Brad Frost's Atomic Design gave teams a shared mental model for composing interfaces from small parts into large ones.2 Salesforce's design system team popularised the term design tokens for named design decisions that can be compiled into any platform's code.3 In October 2025 the W3C Design Tokens Community Group published the first stable version of a vendor-neutral format for those tokens.4 Design systems have moved from a design-team initiative to shared product infrastructure, and the standards have caught up.

01.2Style guide, UI kit, component library, design system

These four terms are not synonyms. Each is a part of a design system, and each has a ceiling on what it can do on its own.

ArtefactWhat it isLives inPrimary usersWhat it cannot do alone
Style guideWritten rules for the brand and visual language: logo, colour, typography, imagery, voice.PDF, wiki, brand siteBrand, marketing, designersGuarantee that what ships matches. It describes; it doesn't build.
UI kitReusable visual elements in a design tool: styles, components, icons.Figma (or similar)DesignersReach production. Engineers re-implement it by eye, so the kit and the product drift apart.
Component libraryCoded, reusable UI components with an API (props, variants, states).A code package (e.g. npm)EngineersExplain when and why. Without shared foundations it faithfully reproduces existing inconsistency.
Pattern libraryDocumented solutions to recurring problems: forms, empty states, filtering, onboarding.Docs siteDesigners, PMs, engineersEnforce itself. Patterns are guidance that still has to be built from components.
Design systemAll of the above, connected by tokens, with documentation, ownership and a process for change.Design tool, code, docs, and a teamEveryone who builds the productSucceed without adoption. It is only as real as the share of the product built with it.

Common mistake

Calling a Figma library a design system

It is an easy and costly confusion. Leadership believes the consistency problem is solved; engineering, which never received anything it could import, keeps building its own versions. A UI kit is a legitimate and often correct first step (Chapter 02 explains when). Just call it what it is, so nobody budgets as if production is covered.

Which one do you have today?

Answer honestly. Each "no" marks the edge of what you currently have.

  • Our colours, type sizes and spacing values exist as named tokens, not just hex codes in a file.
  • Engineers import components from a shared package rather than rebuilding them per team.
  • The design library and the code library use the same names for the same things.
  • There is written guidance on when to use each component, not just what it looks like.
  • Someone is accountable for the system, and it is in their job description.
  • Changes are versioned and announced; teams can upgrade on purpose.
  • Teams know how to propose a new component or change an existing one.

Seven yeses and you run a design system. One to three, you have a UI kit or component library with ambitions. That's fine, as long as it's a deliberate stage and not a stall.

01.3The anatomy of a complete design system

A complete system has six layers that build on one another, and three capabilities that cut across all of them. Each layer only references the layer below it. That one-directional dependency is what lets a change at the bottom flow safely to the top.

LayerContainsWho decidesChanges how often
Principles3–5 statements that settle trade-offs ("clarity over density", "accessible by default").Design and product leadershipRarely; years
FoundationsColour, typography, spacing, grid, elevation, radius, motion, iconography. The subject of Part 02.System team, with brandRarely; each change is high-impact
TokensNamed, platform-agnostic values: primitive, semantic, component.System teamOccasionally; via versioned releases
ComponentsButtons, inputs, tables, dialogs, each with variants, states, API and a11y behaviour.System team plus contributorsContinuously; minor releases
PatternsCompositions solving a user problem: search and filter, bulk actions, error recovery.System team plus product teamsContinuously
TemplatesPage scaffolds and layouts built from components and patterns.Product teams, curated by systemAs products evolve

A complete system does not mean a large one. A startup's complete system might be one page of principles, 120 tokens and 15 components, and still have all six layers and all three capabilities. Completeness is about connection, not volume.

01.4How a design system connects the whole organisation

The most underrated function of a design system is linguistic. It gives design, engineering and product one vocabulary for the interface. When a designer says "primary button", an engineer types <Button variant="primary">, and both resolve to the token color.action.primary, a whole category of handoff error disappears.

FunctionWithout a systemWith a working system
DesignRe-solves the same table, form and empty state on every project. Specs every pixel in handoff.Assembles known parts and spends time on the problems that are actually new.
EngineeringBuilds a "new" button per team; fixes the same focus bug in five places.Imports tested components; fixes a bug once and ships the fix everywhere.
ProductEstimates swing because UI scope is unknown; design QA becomes a release gate.UI scope is predictable; teams talk about behaviour, not padding.
BusinessA rebrand is a multi-quarter programme; accessibility is a recurring audit finding.Brand and accessibility changes are made at the token layer and released.

01.5Why design systems matter more as products scale

A design system's value is not linear in company size. It compounds, for two reasons you can reason about without any vendor statistics.

Reason one: coordination grows faster than headcount

If every team that makes UI decisions has to stay consistent with every other team, the number of pairwise agreements grows as n(n−1)/2. That is the communication-path arithmetic Fred Brooks described for software teams.5 Four teams need six agreements. Sixteen teams need 120. If instead each team agrees with one shared system, the number of agreements grows only as n.

Reason two: the cost of change multiplies

Without tokens, changing a brand colour means finding every hard-coded value across every codebase, platform and design file: roughly products × platforms × occurrences. With a token architecture, it means changing one value and releasing. The same applies to an accessibility fix, a new dark theme or a typography refresh. The more surfaces you have, the more each "change once" saves. That's why the clearest returns usually appear at the second product, the second platform or the first rebrand, not at the first component.

This is the kind of problem design systems exist to solve. At CARS24, for example, the work Layer One's founder led put more than ten products in three countries on one colour and token system.1 That outcome is only practical with a token layer between decisions and code.

Practice Layer One view

Judge a design system by what it makes cheap

Good systems make the common case fast (building a standard screen) and the expensive case cheap (changing a decision everywhere). If yours does neither, it is a catalogue, not a system.

Glossary: the ten terms this playbook uses precisely

FoundationA category of fundamental visual decision: colour, typography, spacing, layout, elevation, motion.
Design tokenA named design decision stored in a platform-agnostic format and compiled into code (space.400 = 16px).
Primitive tokenA raw value with a descriptive name and no usage intent (color.blue.600).
Semantic tokenA token named for its purpose that points to a primitive (color.text.link → color.blue.700).
ComponentA reusable piece of UI with a defined API, variants, states and accessibility behaviour.
VariantA sanctioned alternative form of a component (primary, secondary, destructive).
PatternA reusable solution to a recurring user problem, composed of components.
ThemeA complete mapping of semantic tokens to values (light, dark, a brand).
AdoptionThe share of the shipped product built with the system, measured in code, not in Figma.
ContributionA change to the system proposed or built by someone outside the core team.

Chapter 02

Who needs a design system, and when

Every product already has a design system. It just might be implicit, inconsistent and stored in people's heads. The real question is how much of it to make explicit, and when.

Read this if

You are deciding whether to invest now, later or not at all, or you are being asked to justify a system to someone who thinks it is premature.

What you'll leave with
  1. Direct answers to the seven questions founders and leaders ask most.
  2. A five-stage maturity model to place your organisation, and to see the next stage.
  3. A decision tree and readiness checklist you can use in a planning meeting.

02.1The seven questions everyone asks

These answers are direct by design. Each one names the condition under which it would change.

Does every company need a design system?

Every company needs consistent design decisions. Not every company needs a dedicated, formal system.

Any product with more than one screen has made decisions about colour, type, spacing and behaviour. The question is whether those decisions are written down, shared and reusable, or re-made by whoever builds the next screen. A two-person team with one product can stay consistent through conversation. Once decisions are made by people who don't talk daily, implicit systems start to fork. Practice

Is a design system only for enterprises?

No. Small companies run them too, at a smaller scale.

zeroheight's 2025 survey of design system practitioners found dedicated teams averaging about three people at companies with fewer than 100 employees, rising to about nine at companies with 500+.6 Documented (The sample is self-selected: people who answer a design systems survey tend to have one.) Enterprises need more governance, not more system. The core of a small system and a large one is the same: foundations, tokens and the components you use most.

Does a startup need product–market fit first?

Before product–market fit, build foundations, not a system.

Pre-PMF, the product will change shape, so investing in a broad component library and governance is waste. But a token layer (named colours, a type scale, a spacing scale) costs days, not months, and it makes pivots cheaper: restyling a product built on tokens is a configuration change. Use an off-the-shelf component library (Radix, MUI and similar) themed with your own tokens, and defer custom components until the product stabilises. Practice

Is a team of 5–6 designers big enough?

Usually yes. But count engineers and surfaces, not designers.

Five designers on one product with eight engineers can stay coherent with a well-maintained UI kit and a shared token file. Five designers serving 40 engineers across a web app, a mobile app and an admin tool cannot. They will spend their week answering "which grey is it?" in Slack. The trigger for a real system is the number of places UI gets built, and how far apart they are. Practice

When is a UI kit enough instead of a full system?

When the problem is design consistency, not delivery consistency.

  • One product, one platform, one codebase, and fewer than about three squads.
  • Engineering already uses a themed third-party component library.
  • Designers disagree with each other more than design disagrees with code.

A UI kit fixes design-to-design drift. It does nothing for design-to-code drift. When the second problem appears, the kit has reached its ceiling.

How do we know we've outgrown what we have?

When the cost of inconsistency shows up in delivery, not just in design reviews.

The signals checklist in 02.4 is the practical test. If you tick five or more, the case for a system is already being paid for, just in rework instead of in investment.

When is a design system unnecessary or premature?

When nobody will own it, nobody will adopt it, or the product won't live long enough to benefit.

  • You are still searching for the product and expect to rebuild the UI within six months.
  • One designer and one or two engineers build everything, and they sit together.
  • The product is a marketing site or a campaign with a short life.
  • Engineering leadership has not agreed to adopt it. A design-only system is a UI kit with a bigger budget.
  • No one can be given protected time to own it. An unowned system decays faster than no system, because people stop trusting it.

02.2A maturity model: where you are, and what's next

Design system maturity is a staircase, not a switch. Most organisations should aim for the next stage, not the last one. Skipping stages usually means building governance for components nobody uses yet.

StageYou know you're here when…The move to the next stageInvestment to get there
0 ImplicitDesigners ask each other for hex codes; engineers inspect screenshots.Define foundations; publish a UI kit with styles.1–3 weeks of one designer
1 Shared stylesDesign is consistent; code still has many values that "look close".Tokens as a single source of truth for design and code; build the most-used components.1–3 months, a designer and an engineer, part-time
2 Foundations in codeNew screens use the package; old ones don't; nobody owns requests.Named owners, docs, release process, contribution path.A small dedicated core (1.5–3 FTE)
3 Managed systemMultiple teams contribute; adoption is measured; releases are routine.Theming, multi-platform output, governance across business units.A dedicated team plus federated contributors
4 PlatformThe system is infrastructure, with its own roadmap, SLAs and metrics.Sustain; reduce cost of change; automate compliance.Ongoing product-level budget

Ranges are Practice estimates for orientation; Chapter 04 builds them up from roles and assumptions.

02.3The decision tree

If you only have ten minutes in a leadership meeting, use this. It intentionally asks about engineering and surfaces before it asks about design.

02.4Signs you have outgrown your current UI infrastructure

Each of these is observable, and most can be counted. Count them before you build the business case; they will become your baseline metrics in Chapter 03.

In the code

  • A search for hard-coded hex values returns hundreds of unique colours.
  • There is more than one Button (or Modal, or Table) component in the codebase.
  • The same accessibility bug (focus, contrast, labels) has been fixed in several places.
  • Engineers estimate a brand colour change in weeks, not hours.
  • Front-end PR reviews regularly argue about spacing and styling.

In the organisation

  • Design QA has become a release gate that blocks shipping.
  • New designers or engineers take weeks to learn "how we do UI here".
  • Customers or sales mention that products "feel like different companies".
  • A second product, platform, brand or acquisition is on the roadmap.
  • Enterprise deals now include accessibility conformance requirements.

Practice How to read your score

0–2: keep doing what you're doing; write down your foundations. 3–5: you are paying for inconsistency in rework; plan Stage 2. 6+: the system is already costing you more by its absence than it would by its presence. Start with an audit to size it.

02.5Four scenarios

These are composite, fictional scenarios. They are not clients; they illustrate how the decision tree resolves in different contexts. Illustrative

Scenario A — Seed fintech

2 designers, 6 engineers, pre-PMF

Situation: one web app, pivoting monthly. The founder wants a "design system like Stripe's".

Recommendation: no system yet. Spend a week defining colour, type and spacing tokens; theme an open-source component library. Why: the product will change, and the tokens will survive the change while bespoke components won't.

Scenario B — Series B SaaS

7 designers, 45 engineers, 2 products

Situation: a web app plus a newly acquired analytics product with its own UI stack. Three button styles; dark mode requested by customers.

Recommendation: Stage 2→3. A two-week audit, then a semantic token layer that themes both products, and 15–20 shared components. Core team of ~2 FTE plus named contributors.

Scenario C — Enterprise internal tools

30+ tools built by different vendors

Situation: every tool looks different; accessibility is a compliance requirement; nobody owns UI centrally.

Recommendation: start with tokens and an accessibility baseline, not components. Tokens can be retro-fitted into legacy stacks; components can't. Establish a hybrid team model and a contribution path vendors must follow.

Scenario D — Brand and marketing site

Agency-built, redesigned every 2–3 years

Situation: the marketing team asks for a design system for the website.

Recommendation: a style guide plus a small set of CMS blocks is the right tool. Share colour and type tokens with the product so the brand stays aligned, but don't fund a product-grade system for a site with a short life.

02.6Readiness checklist

Use this before committing budget. A "no" doesn't mean don't proceed. It means that item becomes the first workstream.

  • Sponsor. A leader with budget authority who will defend the system in planning.
  • Engineering commitment. Engineering leadership agrees teams will adopt the package.
  • Owner. A named person with protected time; ownership is in the job description.
  • Audit. You know what exists today: styles, components, tokens, a11y gaps.
  • Pilot team. One product team volunteers to build with the system first.
  • Baseline metrics. You've counted the signals in 02.4, so you can show change.
  • Scope. You've chosen the next stage, not the final one.
  • Tech stack. You know which frameworks and platforms the system must output to.

Audit before you build.Rule #2 — Layer One

Chapter 03

What a design system is worth

"Consistency and efficiency" is not a business case. This chapter separates what has actually been measured from what is merely claimed, and gives you a way to measure your own outcomes.

Read this if

You need to justify investment to a CFO, a board or a sceptical engineering leader, or you need to prove that an existing system is working.

What you'll leave with
  1. An honest picture of the published evidence, including its limits.
  2. The mechanism behind each of nine business outcomes, so you can argue causally rather than by anecdote.
  3. A KPI framework with formulas you can baseline this quarter.

03.1Where the value actually comes from

Every business benefit of a design system traces back to three mechanisms. If a claimed benefit can't be traced to one of them, be suspicious of it.

Mechanism 1

Decide once

Teams stop re-making the same decisions: which grey, how much padding, how errors behave. Time moves from re-deciding to the problems that are actually new.

Mechanism 2

Build once

Components are built, tested and made accessible once, then reused. Defects are fixed once and the fix ships everywhere.

Mechanism 3

Change once

Because products reference tokens and components rather than copies, a decision changed at the source propagates: rebrands, themes, accessibility fixes.

The first two produce savings that accrue steadily with usage. The third produces savings in lumps, at the moments of change, and it is often the larger of the three over a product's lifetime. Business cases that only count the first two undersell the system; business cases that promise the third without a token architecture overpromise it.

03.2The evidence, honestly

The public evidence base for design system ROI is thinner than the marketing around it suggests. Many percentages in circulation trace back to a small number of studies, several of them run by vendors. That doesn't mean the benefits aren't real. It means you should rely on the mechanisms and measure your own outcomes, rather than borrowing someone else's number.

34%faster completion of a design task when participants had a relevant, up-to-date design system.Documented Figma internal experiment.7 Vendor-run; limited sample detail.
47%faster to code a simple form with IBM's Carbon system than from scratch (median 2 h vs 4.2 h).Documented Sparkbox.8 n = 8 developers; scratch build always done first.
79.1%of the top million home pages had low-contrast text, the most common detectable WCAG failure.Documented WebAIM Million 2025.9 A problem tokens can solve at source.
Evidence ledger — what is known, and how strongly
FindingSource and methodCaveatsHow to use it

Low contrast is the most common accessibility failure on the webWebAIM automated scan of 1M home pages, 2025.9Automated detection only; measures home pages, not apps.To justify contrast-checked colour tokens (Chapter 07).
Most practitioner organisations now fund a dedicated system teamzeroheight Design Systems Report 2025; 294 respondents; 79% report a dedicated team.6Self-selected sample of design-system practitioners.As context for team-size benchmarks, not as proof of ROI.
Visual design shapes perceived usability and credibilityKurosu & Kashimura (1995), the "aesthetic-usability" study;10 Fogg et al. (2003), 2,500+ participants rating web credibility.11Neither study is about design systems. They show that look and coherence affect trust; a system is one way to deliver coherence.To explain why consistency is a revenue issue, not a cosmetic one.

Common mistake

Putting someone else's percentage in your business case

"Design systems make teams 47% faster" will be challenged by the first engineer who reads the study, and your credibility goes with it. Use published findings to show the mechanism is real, then build your case on your own baseline using the KPIs in 03.4. Chapter 04 shows how to do this with conservative assumptions.

03.3Nine outcomes, and the mechanism behind each

For each outcome below, the mechanism column is the argument you make to leadership; the measure column is how you prove it later.

OutcomeMechanismWhat to measureEvidence
Design and delivery velocityDecide once: designers assemble known parts and spec less in handoff.Time from brief to dev-ready design for comparable features; handoff comment count.Documented
Engineering efficiencyBuild once: no re-implementing standard UI; less styling code to review.Cycle time for UI-heavy tickets; lines of custom CSS per feature; PR review rounds on styling.Documented
Reuse, less duplicationOne implementation per component instead of one per team.Number of distinct implementations of the same component across repos; % of UI imported from the package.Practice
Quality and consistencyTested components with defined states; tokens remove "close enough" values.UI defects per release; unique hard-coded colour and spacing values over time.Documented
Accessibility and complianceContrast, focus, target size and semantics are solved in the system and inherited.Automated a11y violations per page; audit findings per release; time to remediate.Standard
Maintenance and scalabilityChange once: a fix or update in the system reaches every consumer through a version bump.Effort (hours) for a cross-product visual change; time to ship a new theme.Practice
Cross-team collaborationA shared vocabulary removes translation between design and code.Survey: "I know which component to use"; design–eng clarification threads per feature.Practice
Time to marketNew products and features start from a working kit instead of a blank page.Time from project start to first usable prototype or beta for new products.Practice
Product trust and perceived qualityCoherent, polished interfaces are judged more usable and credible.Perceived-quality questions in product surveys; support tickets citing confusion; sales feedback.Documented

Evidence column: Documented where published studies support the mechanism (03.2); Standard where a standard defines the requirement (WCAG 2.212); Practice where the case rests on practice and your own measurement.

Accessibility deserves its own line in the budget

Accessibility is the outcome where the business case has moved fastest. WCAG 2.2 sets testable success criteria for contrast, focus visibility and target size.12 Standard Regulation increasingly references these criteria: the European Accessibility Act, for example, applies to many digital products and services placed on the EU market from 28 June 2025.13 A design system is the most efficient place to meet them, because a contrast-checked colour token or a component with correct focus behaviour fixes the issue in every product that uses it. Remediating screen by screen fixes it once, and only until the next screen is built.

03.4A KPI framework you can baseline this quarter

Measure time saved, not usage.Rule #8 — Layer One

Usage metrics (component import counts, Figma insertions) tell you whether the system is used. They don't tell you whether it is worth it. Track both, but report outcomes to leadership.

KPIFormulaHow to collectCadence
AdoptionUI files importing the system ÷ all UI filesStatic analysis of imports across reposMonthly
Token coverage1 − (hard-coded colour + spacing values ÷ total style values)Lint rule or a scripted search for raw valuesMonthly
DuplicationDistinct implementations of component XCode search for known component patternsQuarterly
UI cycle timeMedian(ticket start → merge) for UI tickets, system vs non-systemIssue tracker plus PR data, taggedQuarterly
Design QA defectsVisual + a11y defects found after dev ÷ features shippedBug tracker labelsPer release
AccessibilityAutomated violations per page (axe or similar)CI accessibility checks on key flowsPer release
Cost of changeHours to ship a cross-product visual changeTime-box and log real changes (e.g. a colour update)Per event
Contribution healthMedian days from proposal to release; proposals per quarterContribution trackerQuarterly
Satisfaction% agree: "The system makes my work faster"Short survey of designers and engineersTwice a year

Practice Baselining tip

Measure before you build

Run the duplication, token-coverage and a11y counts during the audit, before any system work ships. Without a baseline, every later number is an opinion. With one, a single slide ("unique colour values: 412 → 61") does more for continued funding than any industry statistic.

03.5When value shows up, and when it doesn't

When a design system destroys value

  • Nobody adopts it. A system with 10% adoption has all of the cost and almost none of the benefit. Adoption is the multiplier on every outcome above.
  • It is too abstract. Components with 40 props that try to serve every case are slower to use than writing the UI by hand.
  • It is a bottleneck. If every new need waits weeks for the system team, product teams will route around it, and they will be right to.
  • It is frozen. A system that doesn't evolve with the product becomes a constraint teams fight rather than a tool they use.

Chapter 05 is about the operating model that prevents all four.

Chapter 04

The economics of design systems

The biggest misconception about design systems is that they need a large upfront investment. They don't. Investment is a dial, not a switch. This chapter shows how to set the dial and how to know when to turn it up.

Read this if

You need a budget number, a staffing plan or an ROI model, or someone has quoted you a seven-figure estimate and you want to understand what drives it.

What you'll leave with
  1. The ten factors that drive cost, so you can scope rather than guess.
  2. Three budget scenarios built from roles and FTE-months, with every assumption stated.
  3. An ROI model you can run with your own numbers, plus an honest view of when it breaks even.

04.1How to read the numbers in this chapter

Salaries differ by a factor of five or more between markets, so a dollar figure from one market is meaningless in another. This chapter therefore budgets in FTE-months (one full-time person for one month) and converts to currency only at the end, using three example rates you should replace with your own.

Illustrative All figures in this chapter are illustrative

They are built from stated assumptions, not measured from real projects. The point is the method: change the assumptions to match your organisation and the model recalculates. The full model is in scripts/generate-data.mjs in the playbook's repository.

04.2What determines the investment

Ten factors explain most of the difference between a system that costs a few FTE-months and one that costs a hundred.

Cost driverLower cost when…Higher cost when…Impact
PlatformsWeb onlyWeb + iOS + Android (+ desktop): each needs native componentsVery high
FrameworksOne front-end frameworkReact and Angular and a legacy stack in parallelVery high
Brands and themesOne brand, light modeDark mode, multiple brands, white-label for customersHigh
Existing debtYoung product, little UI codeYears of divergent UI to migrateHigh
Component scope15–25 core components60+ components including complex data tables, charts, editorsHigh
Accessibility targetWCAG 2.2 AA built in from the startRetrofitting AA (or AAA) onto existing componentsMedium
Documentation depthUsage guidance and code examplesFull public docs site, content guidelines, tutorialsMedium
Team distributionCo-located, one time zoneMany teams, vendors, time zonesMedium
Tooling and automationManual token export, simple packageToken pipeline, visual regression tests, linting, Figma–code syncMedium (pays back)
Governance overheadOne product team as ownerCouncils, multiple business units, compliance sign-offMedium

Platforms and frameworks dominate. Every additional platform roughly means another implementation of every component. That's why token architecture comes first: tokens are the one layer that is written once and compiled to every platform.

04.3Roles and resources

RoleResponsible forWhen you need it
System lead / product ownerRoadmap, prioritisation, stakeholder alignment, adoption, metrics. Treats the system as a product.From Stage 2; can be 0.5 FTE of a design or engineering lead
System designerFoundations, component design, states, documentation of usage, Figma libraries.From Stage 1
System engineer (front end)Token pipeline, component code and API, testing, release and package management.From Stage 1. The role most often missing.
Native engineersiOS and Android component implementations from the same tokens.When you ship native apps
Accessibility specialistStandards, audits, screen-reader testing, review of component behaviour.Part-time from Stage 2
Content / docsDocs site structure, writing guidelines, UX writing patterns.Part-time from Stage 3
ContributorsProduct designers and engineers who propose and build changes.From Stage 3; time protected in their teams' plans

Common mistake

Staffing a design system with designers only

It produces an excellent Figma library and no adoption, because adoption happens in code. Our rule of thumb is at least as much engineering capacity as design capacity on the core team, and more once you ship multiple platforms. Practice

04.4How long it takes

04.5Three budget scenarios

Each scenario lists year-one effort by role, then converts the total at three example loaded monthly costs per person (salary plus overheads): $6,000, $12,000 and $20,000. These are example inputs, not market data; substitute your own. Illustrative

Reading the scenarios

  • The startup system costs less than one engineer for a year. It buys tokens, a themed off-the-shelf library and a handful of custom components: enough to stay coherent through Series A.
  • The mid-sized system is a small team, not a department. Two to three people are enough if the scope is one platform plus mobile web and product teams contribute.
  • Enterprise cost is driven by platforms and brands. Engineering is over half of the enterprise effort here, and native iOS and Android work alone is more than a fifth of it.

04.6Dedicated team or existing product team?

Embedded ownership (product team owns it)Dedicated core team
How it worksOne designer and one engineer get protected time (often 20–30%) to own the system within their product team.A team whose product is the system, serving product teams as customers.
StrengthsCheap; close to real needs; no "ivory tower".Focus; consistent quality; can serve many teams and platforms.
RisksProtected time gets eaten by product deadlines; system bends toward one product.Distance from product reality; becomes a bottleneck if it doesn't enable contribution.
FitsOne product, fewer than ~30 engineers, Stage 1–2.Two or more products or platforms, ~40+ engineers, Stage 3+.

For comparison, zeroheight's 2025 survey reports average dedicated team sizes of about three people at companies under 100 employees, four at 100–499, and nine at 500+.6 Documented Teams rarely grow beyond 20–25 people, even in very large organisations, because at that scale contribution from product teams does the scaling.

04.7Ongoing maintenance costs

The most expensive mistake in design system budgeting is funding the build and not the run. A system without maintenance degrades within a year: components lag behind product needs, teams fork them, and adoption reverses.

What "run" includes

  • Bug fixes and accessibility fixes in components
  • New variants and components as products evolve
  • Dependency and framework upgrades (e.g. a React major version)
  • Design tool library maintenance and releases
  • Documentation, office hours, onboarding
  • Reviewing and merging contributions
  • Measuring adoption and health

Practice Budget run as a team, not a percentage

Rather than "maintenance = X% of build", plan for the team that built the system to stay, at a similar or slightly smaller size, with its time shifting from building to enabling. In our experience, systems whose builders are reassigned after launch rarely keep adoption.

04.8Calculating ROI

A defensible ROI model has three parts: hours saved by reuse, avoided costs at moments of change, and the cost of the team. The formulas:

// Annual value from reuse (efficiency)
hours_saved = people × focused_hours × UI_share × adoption × efficiency_gain
value       = hours_saved × loaded_hourly_rate

// Annual value from change-once events (count only those actually planned)
avoided     = Σ (cost_without_system − cost_with_system) for rebrands, themes, a11y fixes

// Return
ROI         = (value + avoided − system_cost) ÷ system_cost

A worked example: Ledgerly

Ledgerly, our fictional B2B finance product, has 40 engineers and 6 designers. We assume a 20% efficiency gain on work the system covers. That is deliberately well below the 34% and 47% figures from 03.2, which come from best-case tasks. Adoption ramps over three years. We count only efficiency savings, so the model leaves out every change-once event.

That result is deliberately unflattering, and it is the most useful number in this chapter. It shows that at 40 engineers, efficiency alone barely justifies a two-person dedicated team. The case rests on adoption speed and on change-once events, which is exactly where to focus the plan.

04.9Start small, invest progressively

Fund each stage from the evidence produced by the last one. Each step has a gate: a measurable condition that unlocks the next round of investment.

  1. Audit — 2 weeks

    Inventory styles, components and tokens in design and code; baseline duplication, token coverage and accessibility. Gate: leadership agrees on the ranked problem list.

  2. Foundations and tokens — 1–2 months, 1–2 people part-time

    Colour, type, spacing, layout and elevation tokens in code and design. Gate: one product team ships new work using only tokens.

  3. The ten most-used components — 2–3 months

    Pick by frequency in the audit, not by what's interesting. Gate: pilot team measurably faster or fewer UI defects.

  4. Docs, releases and contribution — ongoing

    Make it usable by teams who didn't build it. Gate: a second team adopts without hand-holding; first external contribution merged.

  5. Scale — themes, platforms, governance

    Only now invest in multi-brand, native platforms and formal governance. Gate: adoption above ~60% and a planned change-once event that needs it.

The economics in one sentence

Tokens are cheap and pay back immediately; components pay back with adoption; governance pays back with scale. Fund them in that order.

Chapter 05

Design system operating models

A design system is not something a team builds and publishes. It is a product with users, a roadmap, releases, support and metrics. The operating model decides whether it is still trusted in three years.

Read this if

You are setting up a system team, your system has adoption problems, or product teams see the system team as a bottleneck.

What you'll leave with
  1. A clear choice between centralised, federated and hybrid models, and what each requires.
  2. Working templates: decision rights (RACI), contribution flow, versioning policy.
  3. A health scorecard and a plan for managing design and technical debt.

05.1Treat the system as a product

The most reliable predictor of a healthy design system is whether its team behaves like a product team. That means it knows its users (product designers and engineers), runs discovery on their problems, prioritises a roadmap, ships on a cadence, supports what it ships and measures outcomes.

Product practiceIn a design system team
UsersProduct designers, engineers, PMs, content designers, and sometimes vendors and partners.
DiscoveryAudit requests, sit with product teams, review what teams build outside the system and why.
RoadmapPublic, prioritised by reach (how many teams) × pain, not by what the system team finds interesting.
ReleasesVersioned, with changelogs and migration notes; on a predictable cadence.
SupportA channel with response targets, office hours, onboarding sessions.
MetricsAdoption, coverage, contribution, satisfaction and outcome KPIs (03.4).

05.2Centralised, federated and hybrid models

Nathan Curtis's 2015 essay set out the vocabulary most teams still use: solitary, centralised and federated.14 Salesforce later described a cyclical hybrid, with a central team plus a federated group of contributors that inform each other.15 Curtis himself later concluded that successful systems always have a central team and seek participation from a federated community.16 Documented

ModelStrengthsFailure modeFits
SolitaryFast; grounded in real product needs.The system bends to one product; others don't adopt.Stage 1–2; a single product
CentralisedFocus, consistent quality, clear accountability.Becomes a bottleneck and drifts from product reality ("overlords don't scale").Early Stage 3, while foundations stabilise
FederatedSpreads load; strong product context.Nobody's job, so nobody does it; decisions stall.Rarely works alone
HybridCore quality plus contribution at scale.Needs real investment in contribution process and reviewer time.Stage 3–4; multiple products

Practice Our recommendation

Start solitary or centralised to establish foundations and the first components. Move to hybrid as soon as two or more teams are adopting. Do it deliberately, by budgeting contributor time in product teams' plans, not by hoping for goodwill.

05.3Ownership and decision rights

Most system conflicts are really unclear decision rights. Write them down. The RACI below is a starting template for a hybrid model. Responsible does the work, Accountable makes the call, Consulted gives input, Informed is told.

DecisionSystem leadSystem designersSystem engineersProduct teamsDesign / eng leadership
Change a foundation (palette, type scale)ARCCC
Add a new component to the coreARRCI
Add a variant to an existing componentIARR—
Component API and breaking changesCCA/RCI
Accessibility conformance of componentsARRII
Use of a local (non-system) componentICCA/R—
Deprecate and remove a componentARRCI
System roadmap and fundingRCCCA

Note row six. Product teams are accountable for their own local components. A healthy system lets teams build outside it when it doesn't meet their need. It just asks them to say so, so the system can learn.

05.4Design and engineering collaboration

Design–engineering friction in a system usually comes from two sources of truth disagreeing. Resolve it by deciding, explicitly, what each source is authoritative for.

Tokens

Truth for values

One token source (JSON in the repository, in the DTCG format) feeds both the design tool and code.17 Neither side hand-edits values.

Code

Truth for behaviour

States, keyboard interaction, responsiveness and accessibility semantics are defined by the shipped component.

Design library

Truth for intent

Usage, composition and visual specification. It mirrors code names and variants one-to-one.

One definition of done for a component

  • Designed for every state: default, hover, focus, active, disabled, loading, error, empty.
  • Built using tokens only. No raw values in component code.
  • Keyboard and screen-reader behaviour specified and tested; meets WCAG 2.2 AA.12
  • Names, variants and properties identical in the design library and in code.
  • Documented: when to use, when not to, anatomy, examples, accessibility notes.
  • Released in a versioned package with a changelog entry.

05.5Contribution and review

Contribution is what lets a small core team serve a large organisation. It only works if the path is clear, proportional to the size of the change, and fast.

The rule of two

A component enters the core system when at least two teams need it. Until then, it lives as a local component in the team that built it, built from system tokens so it can be promoted later. This prevents the core from filling with one-off components, and it gives the system a natural pipeline of tested candidates. Practice

05.6Governance and decision-making

Governance is how a system decides when people disagree. Keep it lightweight and written down:

  1. Principles settle most arguments

    "Accessible by default" and "clarity over density" end debates faster than any committee.

  2. RFCs for significant changes

    A one-page proposal (problem, options, recommendation, migration impact) open for comment for a fixed period, decided by the accountable owner.

  3. A small council for cross-org decisions

    At Stage 4, representatives of major product areas meet on a fixed cadence for decisions that affect everyone: foundations, breaking changes, roadmap.

  4. A documented exception path

    Teams may diverge with a stated reason. Exceptions are logged and reviewed quarterly; recurring exceptions become roadmap items.

Every decision comes with a reason.Rule #6 — Layer One

05.7Versioning and release management

Product teams need to upgrade on purpose, not discover changes in production. Use semantic versioning:18 MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH, and define what each means for a design system. Visual changes are the grey area most policies forget.

BumpMeaningDesign system examples
MAJORConsumers must change their code or will see breaking behaviour.Renamed or removed token; changed component API; removed variant; changed default size or spacing that alters layouts.
MINORNew capability, backward compatible.New component, variant, token or icon; new optional property.
PATCHFixes, no intended visual or API change.Bug fix; accessibility fix that doesn't change layout; documentation.

Release practice

  • A predictable cadence (e.g. minor releases every two weeks), with patches as needed.
  • Changelog entries written for consumers ("what changes for you"), not for the system team.
  • Design library versions published in step with code releases.
  • Visual regression tests on every component before release.

Deprecation policy

  • Deprecate in a minor release, with a console warning and docs notice.
  • Provide a migration guide, and a codemod where the change is mechanical.
  • Remove only in the next major release, after a stated minimum period.
  • Track usage of deprecated items so you know when removal is safe.

05.8Documentation and adoption

Docs decide adoption.Rule #9 — Layer One

Engineers and designers adopt what they can understand in the five minutes before a deadline. Every component page should answer, in order:

  1. What is it, and when do I use it?

    One sentence, plus when not to use it and what to use instead.

  2. What does it look like?

    Live examples of variants and states.

  3. How do I build with it?

    Copyable code; properties table; design library link.

  1. What do I need to know about accessibility?

    Keyboard behaviour, labelling requirements, known pitfalls.

  2. Do's and don'ts

    Visual examples of correct and incorrect usage.

  3. What changed?

    Version history and migration notes.

Adoption tactics that work

Pilot, then case study

Ship with one team first; publish their before-and-after internally.

Champions

One named designer and engineer per product team who get early access and a direct line.

Office hours

A weekly slot where anyone can bring a screen and get help building it with the system.

Lint rules

Flag raw colour values and deprecated components in code review, automatically.

Codemods

Automate mechanical migrations so upgrades cost minutes, not sprints.

Make the right way easiest

Starter templates and scaffolds that begin with the system already wired in.

05.9Measuring system health

Review a small scorecard monthly with the team and quarterly with leadership. Look for trends, not targets.

DimensionMetricHealthy signalWarning signal
Adoption% of UI files importing the system; % of products on a supported versionRising; most products within one major versionFlat; products stuck on old majors
CoverageToken coverage; local components per productHard-coded values fallingLocal components growing faster than core
QualityOpen bugs; a11y violations; visual regressionsBugs closed faster than openedSame bug class recurring
FlowMedian time from request to release; contribution countDays to weeks; contributions growingMonths; contributions falling to zero
Sentiment"The system makes my work faster" (% agree)Majority agree and risingTeams describe the system as a blocker

05.10Managing technical and design debt

Every system accumulates debt: components that no longer fit, workarounds that became permanent, values that drifted. Debt is normal; invisible debt is the problem.

Debt typeHow it appearsHow to detect it
Detached instancesDesigners break components to make one-off changes.Design-tool analytics on detachments by component
Hard-coded valuesRaw colours, sizes and spacing in product code.Lint rules; scripted search
Forked componentsTeams copy a system component and modify it.Code search for copied component signatures
Deprecated usageOld components still in production after replacement.Import tracking of deprecated items
Inaccessible patternsComponents that pass in isolation but fail in composition.Automated checks on key flows; periodic manual audits
Design–code driftThe design library and code no longer match.Periodic side-by-side review; token sync checks

Practice A debt budget

Keep a visible debt register, and reserve a fixed share of every cycle (we suggest around a fifth) for paying it down. Teams that schedule debt work on a fixed basis rarely need a "big rewrite"; teams that don't usually end up doing one.

Operating model checklist

  • Team model chosen and written down
  • RACI for the eight decisions in 05.3
  • Tokens, code and design library each own a defined truth
  • Definition of done for components
  • Contribution tiers and the rule of two published
  • Versioning policy including visual changes
  • Deprecation policy with minimum notice period
  • Docs template for every component
  • Health scorecard with a monthly review
  • Debt register and debt budget

Leave the team able to run it without us.Rule #10 — Layer One

Building the foundations of a design system

Chapter 06

Understanding design foundations

Foundations are the small set of decisions that every pixel in your product inherits. They are the cheapest part of a design system to build and the most expensive part to get wrong.

Read this if

You are about to define colour, type or spacing for a product, or you need to understand how a design decision becomes code without being re-typed by hand.

What you'll leave with
  1. A clear list of what counts as a foundation, and what doesn't.
  2. An understanding of "blast radius": why foundation changes are high-impact.
  3. The pipeline from a design decision to a token to production code, which the rest of Part 02 fills in.

06.1What foundations are

A foundation is a category of fundamental visual decision that is not itself a component but is used by every component. Public systems differ in naming (Carbon calls them "elements", Material calls them "styles" and "foundations"), but the categories are remarkably consistent.1920

Chapter 07

Colour

Palettes, ramps, semantic roles, themes, contrast.

Chapter 08

Typography

Typefaces, scale, line-height, roles, responsive type.

Chapter 09

Spacing

Base unit, scale, density, component and layout space.

Chapter 10

Grid and layout

Columns, gutters, breakpoints, containers, regions.

Also

Elevation

Also

Shape

Also

Motion
