Also

Iconography

Grid, stroke, sizes and optical alignment.

This edition covers the four foundations with the largest effect on product quality: colour, typography, spacing and layout. The others follow the same architecture and will be covered in a later edition.

06.2Why foundations matter: blast radius

Every decision in a design system has a blast radius: the number of places it affects. A component property affects one component. A foundation affects all of them. That is why foundations are both the highest-leverage and the highest-risk part of the system.

Foundational decisions shape four outcomes:

QualityContrast, legibility and hierarchy are decided here. A type scale with too-small steps produces muddy hierarchy in every screen.
ConsistencyA constrained set of values (say 12 spacing values instead of "whatever looks right") makes consistency the default rather than a review task.
ScalabilityA semantic layer (07.4) makes themes, dark mode and new brands possible without touching components.
Delivery speedFewer choices mean faster decisions. "Which of these 12 spacing values?" is a quicker question than "how many pixels?"

06.3From decision to token to code

The reason foundations can be changed safely is that they are never typed twice. A decision is captured once as a design token, a named value stored in a platform-agnostic format, and compiled into every platform's code by a build step.

A shared format

Until recently every tool used its own token format. In October 2025 the W3C Design Tokens Community Group published version 2025.10 of the Design Tokens Format Module, its first stable specification.417 Documented It defines a JSON format where each token has a $value and a $type, groups nest with dot-path names, and tokens reference each other with curly braces ({color.brand.700}). Note that it is a Community Group report, not a formal W3C Standard; it is nevertheless the format most token tools now converge on. This is what the Ledgerly tokens look like in it:

Practice Tokens first, components second

Rule #4 of how we work, and the most important sequencing decision in a system. Components built before the token layer exists end up with hard-coded values that must be found and replaced later. Tokens built first make every component themeable from day one.

The next four chapters take each foundation in turn, from first principles to tokens. Chapter 11 then shows them working together in one component.

Chapter 07

Colour systems

Colour is the foundation teams get wrong most often, and the one where getting it right pays back fastest. This chapter goes from colour models to a production token architecture, and every value in it is computed, not guessed.

Read this if

You are defining or repairing a palette, adding dark mode or a second brand, or you keep finding contrast failures in audits.

What you'll leave with
  1. Why OKLCH is the right model for building a system palette, and where it still needs checking.
  2. A repeatable method for generating accessible colour ramps, with a complete worked palette.
  3. A three-tier token architecture that makes themes, dark mode and multiple brands a configuration change.

07.1Colour models: how colour is described

A colour model is a way of describing a colour with numbers. The model you build your palette in decides which questions are easy to answer. For a design system the most important question is "is this lighter or darker than that, and by how much?", because that is what contrast, hierarchy and state changes depend on.

ModelDescribes colour asGood forProblem for design systems
RGBAmounts of red, green and blue light (0–255)How screens work; final outputNot human-readable. Nobody can predict what rgb(204 60 0) looks like, or how to make it 10% lighter.
HEXRGB written in base 16 (#cc3c00)Compact; universal in tools and codeThe same as RGB, and even less readable.
HSLHue (angle), saturation, lightnessPicking colours by intuition"Lightness" is not perceived lightness: hsl(60 100% 50%) (yellow) and hsl(240 100% 50%) (blue) claim the same lightness but look nothing alike.
HSV / HSBHue, saturation, value (brightness)Colour pickers in design toolsSame flaw as HSL; "value 100%" is a different perceived brightness for every hue.
OKLCHLightness (0–1), chroma (colourfulness), hue (angle)Building palettes, ramps and themesSome combinations fall outside what screens can show (07.2), and lightness is close to, but not identical with, WCAG contrast.

Perceptual versus non-perceptual

RGB, HSL and HSV are non-perceptual: equal numeric steps do not look like equal steps to the human eye. A perceptual colour space is designed so that numeric distance tracks perceived difference. Oklab, published by Björn Ottosson in 2020, is a perceptual space designed for exactly this.21 OKLCH is the same space in polar form: lightness, chroma and hue. It is part of CSS Color Module Level 4 and supported natively in current browsers as oklch().22 Standard

Lightness, chroma and hue

Lightness L 0 → 1

How light the colour looks. The axis that drives contrast, hierarchy and states. Black is 0, white is 1.

Chroma C 0 → ~0.37

How colourful it is. 0 is grey. Unlike HSL saturation, the maximum depends on hue and lightness.

Hue H 0° → 360°

Which colour family. Every swatch in this row has L 0.70, so they all look equally light.

Why OKLCH is particularly useful for design systems

  1. Predictable lightness

    Step 700 can mean "this lightness" in every hue. So state changes, hierarchy and contrast behave the same across your whole palette.

  2. Independent axes

    Change hue (a new brand) without changing lightness, and so without breaking contrast. In HSL, rotating hue silently changes perceived lightness.

  3. Generated, not hand-picked, ramps

    Ramps become a formula (a lightness curve plus a chroma envelope), so new hues, brands and white-label themes come out consistent.

  1. Better gradients and mixing

    Interpolating in OKLCH avoids the grey, muddy midpoints of sRGB blends (07.7).

  2. Wide-gamut ready

    OKLCH can describe the more vivid colours of Display P3 screens. In sRGB values you can't even write them down.

  3. Native in CSS and the token spec

    oklch() is in CSS Color 4, and the DTCG 2025.10 format can store OKLCH components directly.2217 Tailwind CSS moved its default palette to OKLCH in v4.0.23 Documented

Two caveats that matter

1. Not every OKLCH colour can be displayed. Screens have a gamut, a range of colours they can physically produce. High chroma at very light or very dark lightness often falls outside sRGB. Tools must gamut-map (reduce chroma until the colour fits); our generator does this, and marks each chip where it happened.

2. OKLCH lightness is not WCAG contrast. WCAG 2 contrast is computed from relative luminance, a different formula.24 Equal OKLCH lightness gives similar contrast across hues, not identical. You still validate every pairing. Figure 7.4 shows exactly how close it gets.

07.2Building a palette

Step 1: Establish the primary colour, and separate brand from action

Most palettes start from a brand colour. The first discovery is usually that the brand colour, at its exact brand value, can't be used for text or for buttons with white labels. Layer One's own signal orange, #ff6b3d, is a good example: it has a contrast of 2.83:1 on white, below the 4.5:1 WCAG 2.2 AA minimum for body text and below 3:1 for UI components. On the ink background it reaches 6.87:1. Standard

The answer is not to change the brand. It is to treat the brand colour as a seed for a ramp, and to choose ramp steps by role. The exact brand value is kept for large brand moments (illustration, the logo, dark-background accents), and a darker step from the same ramp is used for interactive elements on light backgrounds. In the palette below, the brand ramp is generated from #ff6b3d (oklch(0.705 0.191 37)), and brand.700 becomes the primary action colour.

Step 2: Choose supporting hues by job, not by taste

A product palette needs far fewer hues than a brand palette. Most products need:

HueJobRule
Brand / primaryPrimary actions, selection, key brand momentsOne hue; not reused for status
NeutralText, surfaces, borders, most of the interfaceLow chroma, often tinted toward the brand or a cool hue
Danger (red)Errors, destructive actionsNever the same hue as brand
Success (green)Confirmation, positive statusAlways paired with an icon or label
Warning (amber)Caution, pending statesDark text on amber, not white
Info / link (blue)Links, informational messages, focus ringsMay double as primary if brand is blue

Status colours must never carry meaning on their own. WCAG 2.2 success criterion 1.4.1 ("Use of Color") requires that colour is not the only visual means of conveying information,12 so every status colour ships with an icon, a label or both. Standard

Watch for collisions between brand and status hues. Ledgerly's brand orange sits at hue 37° and its danger red at 25°, only 12° apart. That's a realistic situation for a warm brand, and it means colour alone could never tell "primary action" from "destructive action". The fix is structural, not chromatic: destructive buttons get an explicit label and confirmation, and errors always carry an icon.

Step 3: Build ramps on a fixed lightness curve

A ramp (also called a scale or tonal palette) is the set of lightness steps for one hue. The key move in OKLCH is to fix the lightness of each step across all hues: blue.700, red.700 and neutral.700 all have L ≈ 0.485. That makes the step number itself meaningful.

Step50100200300400500600700800900950
Lightness L0.9750.9450.8850.8150.7300.6450.5650.4850.4050.3300.255
Chroma × peak0.120.260.500.740.921.001.000.920.780.600.45
Typical roleBackgrounds, tintsSubtle fills, bordersStrong borders, icons, large accentsText-safe accents, actionsText, dark surfaces

The curve is denser at both ends than in the middle. Interfaces need many very light tints (surfaces, hover backgrounds, selected rows) and several very dark values (text, dark-mode surfaces), but only a few mid-tones. Radix Colors takes a similar purpose-led approach with 12 steps, each assigned a job from app background to high-contrast text;25 Material 3 generates tonal palettes from a key colour in its HCT colour space.20 Documented

Step 4: Shape chroma, then fit it to the gamut

Colourfulness should peak in the middle of the ramp and fall away toward both ends. Very light tints with high chroma look neon; very dark shades with high chroma look muddy. Our generator multiplies each hue's peak chroma by an envelope (the second row of the table above), then reduces chroma wherever the result falls outside sRGB. Lightness and hue are preserved, so contrast stays predictable.

Step 5: Validate contrast, and learn the pairing rules

WCAG 2.2 sets three thresholds you'll use constantly:2426 Standard

4.5:1Minimum for body text (AA, SC 1.4.3). 7:1 for AAA (SC 1.4.6).
3:1Large text: at least 18pt, or 14pt bold (about 24px / 18.66px).
3:1Non-text: UI component boundaries, focus indicators, meaningful graphics (SC 1.4.11).

Because lightness is fixed per step, contrast between two steps depends mostly on how many steps apart they are. That gives your team pairing rules they can apply without a contrast checker:

What about APCA?

APCA (the Accessible Perceptual Contrast Algorithm) is a newer contrast method that accounts for font size, weight and polarity, and it has been explored for future versions of WCAG.27 Radix Colors, for example, tunes its text steps to APCA targets.25 It is promising, but WCAG 2.x contrast remains the normative requirement for conformance today. Validate with WCAG 2 ratios, and use APCA as additional guidance for dark mode and thin type if you wish.

07.3Neutrals: the colour you use most

In a typical product, neutrals cover far more of the screen than any other colour: text, backgrounds, surfaces, borders, dividers, disabled states. A carefully built neutral ramp does more for perceived quality than any brand colour.

Pure grey or tinted?

Pure greys (chroma 0) can feel cold and slightly "dead" next to a saturated brand colour. A very small amount of chroma (0.005–0.02 in OKLCH) tinted toward the brand hue (warm) or toward blue (cool) makes neutrals feel intentional. Ledgerly's neutral ramp uses chroma 0.018 at hue 260: a cool, barely visible tint. Practice

How many neutral steps?

Use the same 11 steps as every other ramp so the pairing rules apply. In practice, light themes use about six neutral steps (50, 100, 200, 500, 700, 950) and dark themes about six more. Unused steps are cheap to keep and prevent ad-hoc greys later.

Common mistake

Light grey text

Low-contrast grey text for "secondary" information is the single most common accessibility failure on the web. WebAIM's 2025 scan found low-contrast text on 79.1% of the top million home pages.9 Fix it at the token: color.text.secondary in Ledgerly maps to neutral.700 (5.99:1 on the canvas), never to anything lighter.

07.4Colour architecture: primitive, semantic and component tokens

A palette is a set of values. A colour system is the layer of meaning on top of it. Mature public systems (Atlassian, Carbon, Spectrum, Salesforce Lightning, Material) all separate raw values from usage, even though their names differ.2829303 Documented

Why separate raw values from usage?

Themes become a remap, not a rewrite

Dark mode changes which primitive each semantic token points to. No component changes.

Meaning survives refactoring

If danger moves from red.700 to red.800, you change one reference, not every red in the product.

Decisions are reviewable

"Is text.secondary accessible?" is one check. "Are all the greys used for secondary text accessible?" is an audit.

The palette stays closed

Designers and engineers choose from roles, not from 66 swatches, so new ad-hoc colours stop appearing.

Do you need component tokens?

Component tokens add a level of indirection, and that has a cost: more tokens to name, document and maintain. Use them when (a) you support multiple brands or white-label theming that must restyle specific components, or (b) one component legitimately differs from the semantic default. Otherwise, components can consume semantic tokens directly. Many teams start with two tiers and add the third when theming demands it. Practice

Brand tokens

In a multi-brand system, add a brand tier between primitives and semantics: each brand defines its own primitive ramps (or just its seed hues, from which ramps are generated), and the semantic tier references brand.* rather than a specific hue. Swapping the brand tier restyles every product. With OKLCH-generated ramps, a new brand needs only a seed colour; the lightness curve guarantees the same contrast behaviour.

Naming semantic colour tokens

Use a consistent grammar so people can guess names they haven't seen. Rule #3 of how we work is "name things so people can guess them". A grammar that works across most products:

color.{category}.{role}.{variant?}.{state?}

color.bg.surface                      // backgrounds: canvas, surface, subtle, inverse
color.text.secondary                   // text: primary, secondary, disabled, inverse, link
color.border.strong                    // border: default, strong, focus
color.icon.subtle
color.action.primary.bg.hover         // interactive: role → part → state
color.feedback.danger.text            // status: danger, warning, success, info

Background, surface, border, text and icon colours

CategoryPurposeRule of thumb
BackgroundThe canvas of the app and large regions.Lightest steps in light mode; darkest in dark mode.
SurfaceCards, panels, menus, dialogs sitting on the background.One step of separation from the background, plus a border or elevation.
BorderDividers (decorative) and component boundaries (functional).Decorative borders can be subtle; boundaries of inputs and controls need 3:1.
TextPrimary, secondary, disabled, inverse, link.All except disabled must pass 4.5:1 on every surface they appear on.
IconMeaningful icons and decorative ones.Meaningful icons need 3:1; often share the text tokens.

07.5Interactive and state colours

Interactive elements need a colour for each state: default, hover, pressed (active), focus, selected and disabled. There are two common strategies:

Strategy A — Step shift

Move along the ramp

Hover moves one step darker (light mode) or lighter (dark mode): brand.700 → brand.800. Explicit, easy to check for contrast, and every state is a named token.

DefaultHoverPressedFocus
Strategy B — State layers

Overlay a translucent layer

A semi-transparent layer of the content colour is placed over the component on hover or press. Material Design uses this approach. It works with any background, and fewer tokens are needed.

Default+ hover layer+ press layer

Focus deserves special care. A focus indicator is non-text content that must reach 3:1 against adjacent colours.26 Use a dedicated color.focus.ring token (Ledgerly: blue.600 in light mode, 4.28:1 on the canvas). Don't reuse the brand colour, which may not contrast with the component it surrounds. Disabled elements are exempt from contrast requirements under WCAG, but they should still be legible enough to be recognised. Never rely on disabled styling alone to explain why something can't be used.

07.6Themes: light, dark, brand and white-label

With a semantic tier in place, a theme is simply a complete mapping from semantic tokens to primitives. The figure below shows the same mini-interface built from the same semantic tokens, rendered through two mappings.

Dark mode is not inversion

  • Don't use pure black. Very dark neutral surfaces (Ledgerly: neutral.950, L 0.255) reduce glare and leave room for elevation.
  • Express elevation with lighter surfaces. Shadows barely show on dark backgrounds. Raised surfaces step lighter (neutral.900, neutral.800).
  • Lighten, and often desaturate, accents. Ledgerly's primary action moves from brand.700 to brand.400 in dark mode, with dark text on top (5.96:1).
  • Re-validate everything. Pairings that pass in light mode can fail in dark mode, and vice versa.

Carbon, for example, ships four themes (two light, two dark) from a single set of semantic tokens.29 Documented

Multi-brand and white-label

ScenarioWhat changesArchitecture
Light / darkSemantic → primitive mappingTwo theme files over one palette
Multiple brands you ownBrand primitives; sometimes type and radiusA brand tier, plus light/dark per brand
White-label for customersA small, controlled set of inputs (e.g. one seed colour, a logo)Generate ramps from the seed in OKLCH; expose only those inputs, never raw tokens

Practice White-label safely

Let customers pick a seed colour, then generate their ramp with your lightness curve and map your semantic tokens to it. Because lightness is fixed per step, a customer's "brand.700" lands at the same lightness as yours, so contrast survives a choice you didn't make. Validate the generated pairings automatically and fall back to a darker step where a hue misses (as green does at 600).

07.7Practical questions

How many colours should a design system contain?

Few hues, many steps, and fewer semantic tokens than you expect.

A typical product needs one brand hue, one neutral, and three or four status hues: five to seven ramps. At 11 steps each, that's 55–77 primitives, but only 30–60 semantic tokens, and those are what people actually choose from. Practice

How many shades should a ramp have?

Between 10 and 13 steps is the established range.

Tailwind uses 11 (50–950), Radix 12, and Material's tonal palettes 13 tones.232520 Documented Fewer than about 9 leaves gaps for states and dark mode; more than about 13 produces steps nobody can tell apart.

Is there a maximum number of colours?

There's no standard maximum, but there is a practical one: what your team can tell apart and remember.

The symptom of too many colours isn't the palette size. It's semantic tokens with overlapping meaning (text.muted, text.subtle, text.secondary, text.tertiary). If two tokens can't be explained differently in one sentence, merge them.

How do we stop colour proliferation?
  • Components consume semantic tokens only; lint against raw colour values in product code.
  • New semantic tokens need a reason ("which role doesn't exist yet?") and an owner's approval.
  • Run the "unique colours in code" count from Chapter 03 every quarter. It should fall.
How should we handle gradients?

Interpolate in OKLCH and tokenise the stops.

Blending in sRGB passes through a dull, greyish midpoint; OKLCH keeps the midpoint vivid and evenly bright. CSS lets you choose the interpolation space directly.

linear-gradient(in srgb, blue.600, amber.400)
linear-gradient(in oklch, blue.600, amber.400)
What about overlays and transparency?

Use transparency for overlays and state layers, never for text.

Scrims behind dialogs (color.overlay.scrim → oklch(0.2 0.02 260 / 0.5)) and state layers are good uses of alpha. Text with alpha is not: its contrast changes with whatever is behind it, so it can't be validated once. Give text solid tokens.

Colour system checklist

  • Palette built in OKLCH from a fixed lightness curve
  • Brand colour used as a seed; action colour is a text-safe step
  • 5–7 ramps, 10–13 steps each, same step numbers across hues
  • Gamut mapping applied; hex fallbacks generated, not hand-picked
  • Neutral ramp with a deliberate tint (or a deliberate lack of one)
  • Pairing rules published for designers
  • Primitive and semantic tiers; components never reference primitives
  • Token naming grammar documented
  • State colours defined for every interactive role, including focus
  • Light and dark themes as semantic mappings
  • Every semantic pairing contrast-tested automatically in CI
  • Status colours always paired with icon or text

Chapter 08

Typography systems

Most of any interface is text. A typography system isn't a font choice and a list of sizes. It is a set of roles, a scale, a rhythm and a set of rules that keep text readable on every screen and every platform.

Read this if

You are choosing a typeface, defining a type scale, or your product's hierarchy feels muddy or inconsistent across screens.

What you'll leave with
  1. A method for building a type scale, from ratio to rounded, grid-aligned values.
  2. A complete, tokenised product type scale you can adapt.
  3. Guidance on how typography should differ across SaaS, enterprise, mobile, desktop and data-heavy products.

08.1Choosing typefaces

For product interfaces, typeface selection is primarily a functional decision. Brand expression matters, but it is secondary to legibility at small sizes and coverage of everything the product needs to display.

CriterionWhat to checkWhy it matters
Legibility at small sizesSet 12–14px samples on real screens. Check x-height, open apertures, and distinguishable Il1, O0, rn/m.Labels, tables and captions live at small sizes.
Weights and stylesAt least regular, medium and semibold (or a variable weight axis); true italics if your content needs them.Hierarchy depends on weight as much as size.
NumeralsTabular (fixed-width) figures via font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums; clear distinction between 1 and 7.Columns of numbers must align in tables and dashboards.
Language coverageEvery script you ship or plan to ship: Latin Extended, Cyrillic, Arabic, Devanagari…A fallback font for one market breaks visual consistency.
LicensingWeb, app embedding, and number of products. Open-source (OFL) fonts remove most of the friction.Licence terms can block a platform launch.
PerformanceFile size; variable font versus several static files; subsetting.Fonts are often among the largest assets on first load.

System fonts

Platform UI fonts (San Francisco on Apple platforms, Roboto on Android, Segoe UI on Windows) are highly legible, free, cost nothing to load and feel native. They're the right default for many internal and enterprise tools. The trade-off is weaker brand distinctiveness.

How many families?

One family for UI is usually enough. A second (a mono for code and data, or a display face for marketing) is common. A third is rarely justified in product UI. This playbook uses Schibsted Grotesk for everything and JetBrains Mono for values a machine reads.

Variable fonts

A variable font stores a continuous range of a design axis, most commonly weight, in one file.31 Instead of choosing between four static weights, the system can use any weight between, say, 400 and 900. For a design system this means one file to load, exact weight tokens (font.weight.semibold = 600), and optical adjustments such as slightly heavier weights in dark mode.

08.2Type scale architecture

A type scale is the limited set of font sizes your product uses. The classical method is a modular scale: start from a base size (usually 16px, the browser default) and multiply by a constant ratio for each step up, divide for each step down.

A pure modular scale is a starting point, not the answer. Product interfaces need several sizes clustered between 12 and 20px (labels, body, small headings), and only a few large sizes. A single ratio rarely provides both. Most mature systems therefore start from a ratio and then adjust by hand, rounding to whole pixels and to the line-height grid. Material 3's type scale, for example, is a curated set of 15 named styles rather than a strict geometric progression.32 Documented

Line-height: tighter as text grows

Line-height (leading) should decrease as a ratio as size increases. Body text needs about 1.4–1.6× for comfortable reading; large headings look loose above about 1.2×. Snap every line-height to your spacing grid (4px in this playbook) so text and components align vertically.

Font sizeTarget ratioRule used to generate the scale
≤ 14px≈ 1.45line-height = round(size × ratio ÷ 4) × 4, the nearest multiple of 4px to the target. Small sizes end up slightly looser and large sizes slightly tighter, which is the direction you want. Headings use the tighter ratios at every size, so an 18px heading gets 24px, not the 28px of 18px body text.
15–20px≈ 1.5
21–32px≈ 1.3
33–48px≈ 1.2
> 48px≈ 1.1

Letter-spacing (tracking)

Typefaces are spaced for text sizes. At large sizes, the default spacing looks loose, so display and heading styles usually take slightly negative tracking (around −0.01 to −0.02em). At very small sizes, and in all-caps labels, slightly positive tracking improves legibility. Store tracking in em so it scales with size.

08.3Roles and hierarchy: a complete product scale

Name type styles by role, not by size. "Heading large" survives a redesign; "28px" doesn't. Five role families cover almost every product interface:

Display

Hero numbers, marketing moments, empty-state headlines.

Heading

Page and section titles; the structure of a screen.

Body

Paragraphs, descriptions, table cells, form values.

Label

Buttons, tabs, form labels, navigation. Medium weight.

Caption

Metadata, timestamps, helper text, footnotes.

Hierarchy uses more than size

A common mistake is to create hierarchy with size alone, which inflates the scale. Weight, colour (text.primary vs text.secondary), case and spacing are equally strong signals and cost no new sizes.

✕ Hierarchy by size only

Invoices
Overdue
3 invoices totalling ₹2,40,000
Last reminder sent 2 days ago

✓ Size, weight, colour and space

Invoices
Overdue
3 invoices totalling ₹2,40,000
Last reminder sent 2 days ago

The right-hand version uses fewer sizes but has a clearer hierarchy, because each level differs on two or more dimensions.

08.4Responsive typography

Large display and heading sizes that work on a desktop overwhelm a phone. There are two approaches:

Stepped

Different token values per breakpoint

heading.xl is 28px below 600px wide and 36px above. Simple, predictable, easy to spec in design tools.

Fluid

Interpolate between a minimum and maximum

Size scales smoothly with viewport width using CSS clamp(). Fewer jumps; popularised by tools such as Utopia.33

/* heading.xl: 28px at a 360px viewport → 36px at 1280px */
--type-heading-xl-size: clamp(1.75rem, 1.554rem + 0.87vw, 2.25rem);

/* slope     = (36 − 28) ÷ (1280 − 360) = 0.0087  → 0.87vw
   intercept = 28 − 0.0087 × 360  = 24.87px     → 1.554rem */

Common mistake

Fluid type that ignores zoom

Font sizes set purely in viewport units (font-size: 3vw) don't grow when users zoom, which can fail WCAG 2.2 SC 1.4.4 (Resize Text, up to 200%).12 Standard Always include a rem component in the fluid formula, as above, and only make display and heading sizes fluid. Body text should stay fixed and readable.

Native platforms add their own layer. iOS Dynamic Type and Android's font scaling let users choose larger text system-wide. Apple's guidelines encourage supporting Dynamic Type so text scales with the user's preference.34 A design system for native apps should map each type token to the platform's scalable text style rather than to a fixed size.

08.5Accessibility and readability

RequirementWhat it means for the type systemBasis
Contrast4.5:1 for body text, 3:1 for large text (≥ 24px, or ≥ 18.66px bold). Defined in the colour tokens used by each text style.Standard SC 1.4.324
ResizeText can scale to 200% without loss of content: use relative units and let containers grow.Standard SC 1.4.4
Text spacingLayouts must not break when users override line-height to 1.5×, paragraph spacing to 2×, letter spacing to 0.12em and word spacing to 0.16em. Avoid fixed-height text containers.Standard SC 1.4.1235
ReflowContent reflows to a 320 CSS px width without horizontal scrolling (except tables, maps and similar).Standard SC 1.4.1036
Line lengthAim for about 45–75 characters per line for long-form text; cap reading widths with a max-width in ch.Documented Bringhurst37
Minimum sizesAvoid body text below 14px in dense web UI and 16px on mobile web; reserve 11–12px for captions and labels.Practice

08.6Typography across product categories

The same principles produce different scales for different products. The table summarises how we would tune a type system for each category. Platform defaults are documented; the rest is practice.

CategoryBody sizeScale ratioPrioritiesWatch out for
SaaS web app14–16px~1.2Clear headings for navigation; comfortable forms; 10–14 styles.Marketing-site scales leaking into the app.
Enterprise software14px (13px dense)~1.125–1.2Density and scannability; strong label/value contrast; long sessions.Text so small it fails users with low vision; offer a comfortable density mode.
Mobile appsiOS: 17pt body; Android: 16sp body largePlatform scaleUse platform text styles; support Dynamic Type and font scaling.3432 DocumentedFixed-height rows that truncate when users enlarge text.
Desktop apps13–15px~1.125–1.2Follow OS conventions; dense menus and panels; keyboard-heavy use.Mixing OS and brand fonts inconsistently.
Responsive web16px1.2 mobile → 1.25–1.33 desktopFluid headings; fixed body; readable line length at every width.Headings that wrap to five lines on phones.
Data-heavy dashboards13–14px~1.125Tabular numerals; a "metric" display style; compact labels; mono for IDs.Hierarchy lost in a sea of same-size numbers; use weight and colour.

IBM Carbon formalises a similar split with two type sets: a productive set for dense task-focused product UI and an expressive set for editorial and marketing moments.38 Documented If your product has both a dense app and a marketing surface, consider the same separation rather than one compromise scale.

08.7Typography tokens

Typography uses two token levels. Primitive tokens hold individual values (families, sizes, weights, line-heights, tracking). Composite tokens bundle them into styles by role. The DTCG format defines a composite typography type for exactly this.17

// primitives
"font": {
  "family": { "sans": { "$type": "fontFamily", "$value": ["Schibsted Grotesk", "system-ui", "sans-serif"] } },
  "weight": { "semibold": { "$type": "fontWeight", "$value": 600 } }
},
// composite, by role
"type": { "heading": { "lg": {
  "$type": "typography",
  "$value": {
    "fontFamily": "{font.family.sans}", "fontWeight": "{font.weight.semibold}",
    "fontSize": { "value": 28, "unit": "px" }, "lineHeight": 1.29,
    "letterSpacing": { "value": -0.01, "unit": "em" }
  } } } }

Typography checklist

  • One UI family (plus mono if needed), tested at 12–14px
  • Tabular numerals available and used in tables
  • 10–15 styles named by role, not size
  • Line-heights snapped to the 4px grid
  • Tracking defined in em for display and labels
  • Responsive strategy chosen: stepped or fluid (with rem)
  • Layouts survive 200% text resize and text-spacing overrides
  • Reading widths capped at roughly 45–75 characters
  • Native styles mapped to Dynamic Type / font scaling
  • Composite typography tokens in design tool and code

Chapter 09

Spacing systems

Spacing is the foundation people notice least and feel most. It creates grouping, hierarchy and rhythm. Left to individual judgement, it is also the first thing to drift.

Read this if

Your screens feel "slightly off" without anyone being able to say why, reviews keep debating padding, or you need to support compact and comfortable densities.

What you'll leave with
  1. A base unit and a spacing scale, with the reasoning behind both.
  2. A clear model for component spacing versus layout spacing, and for density modes.
  3. Spacing tokens, and the mistakes to avoid when introducing them.

09.1Why spacing systems matter

Space does three jobs in an interface. It groups related things (the Gestalt principle of proximity: elements close together are read as belonging together). It creates hierarchy, because more space around something gives it more importance. And it sets rhythm, a repeated cadence that makes a screen feel calm and intentional.

When spacing is chosen per screen, each value is defensible on its own, but together they are noise: 13px here, 14px there, 22px somewhere else. Users don't consciously notice the numbers. They notice that the interface feels slightly unresolved.

09.2Choosing a base unit

A spacing system starts with a base unit, and every spacing value is a multiple of it. The two common choices are 8px and 4px.

8px base

Fewer, more distinct values

Easy to reason about; most screen sizes divide by 8. Used by many systems as the primary unit: Atlassian's spacing scale is built on an 8px base, with smaller half and quarter steps for tight UI.39 Documented

4px base

Finer control for dense UI

Allows 12px, 20px and 28px, which matter for small components, icon alignment and line-heights. Material uses a 4dp baseline grid for type and icons alongside its 8dp layout grid.40 Documented

Practice Our recommendation

Use a 4px base with an 8px rhythm: every value is a multiple of 4, and most of the values people reach for are multiples of 8. You get the precision dense components need without the indecision of a scale where every value is available. Align line-heights (Chapter 08) to the same 4px grid so text and boxes share one vertical rhythm.

09.3The spacing scale

A scale is the closed list of spacing values the system offers. It should be dense at the small end, where 4px is a visible difference, and sparse at the large end, where 64px versus 68px is not. A roughly geometric progression does this naturally.

Naming spacing tokens

ConventionExampleProsCons
Multiple of basespace.6 = 24pxGuessable; easy maths; open-endedChanging the base unit renames everything
Multiplier ×100space.300 = 3 × 8px (Atlassian)39Room for fractional steps (space.050)Values less obvious at a glance
Ordinalspacing-06 = 24px (Carbon)19Compact; stable orderMust look up every value
T-shirt sizesspace.mdFriendlyRuns out of names (xxxl); hard to insert steps

Any convention works if it is consistent. Choose the one your engineers can read without a lookup table.

09.4Component spacing and layout spacing

It helps to separate spacing inside components from spacing between them. Nathan Curtis describes three kinds: inset (padding inside a container), stack (vertical space between stacked elements) and inline (horizontal space between elements in a row).41

LevelTypical rangeExamples
Within a componentspace.1–space.4 (4–16px)Icon-to-label gap, button padding, input padding, chip gap
Between related elementsspace.2–space.4 (8–16px)Label to field, field to field, list items
Between groupsspace.6–space.8 (24–32px)Form sections, card grid gaps, toolbar to content
Between sectionsspace.10–space.16 (40–64px)Page sections, settings groups
Page marginsspace.4–space.20 (16–80px)Responsive; see Chapter 10

The proximity rule: space within a group must always be clearly smaller than space between groups. A useful heuristic is to step at least two scale steps between levels (8 → 16 → 24/32). That keeps relationships unambiguous even when designers make reasonable local choices. Practice

09.5Density: compact and comfortable

Density is how much information fits in a given area. Different users and tasks need different density: an analyst scanning 200 rows wants compact; a first-time user filling a form wants comfortable. Systems handle this with density modes that remap component sizes and spacing, not with separate components.

Density has a floor set by accessibility. WCAG 2.2 SC 2.5.8 (Target Size, Minimum, level AA) requires pointer targets of at least 24 × 24 CSS px, with some exceptions such as adequately spaced targets and inline links.42 Standard Platform guidelines go further for touch: Apple recommends at least 44 × 44pt for controls,43 and Material recommends 48 × 48dp touch targets.40 Documented Compact modes are for pointer-driven desktop use; never ship them as the default on touch devices.

TokenCompactDefaultComfortable
size.control.height32px40px48px
space.control.inset-x8px12px16px
space.table.row-y4px8px12px
space.form.stack12px16px24px

09.6Responsive spacing and spacing tokens

Component spacing should generally not change with screen size: a button's padding is the same on a phone and a desktop. Layout spacing should: page margins, section gaps and grid gutters grow with available space. Encode that split in tokens:

/* Tier 1: primitive scale (never changes with breakpoint) */
--space-2: 8px;  --space-4: 16px;  --space-6: 24px;  --space-10: 40px;  --space-16: 64px;

/* Tier 2: semantic layout spacing (responsive) */
--space-page-margin:  var(--space-4);     /* 16px on compact screens   */
--space-section-gap:  var(--space-10);
@media (min-width: 840px) {
  --space-page-margin: var(--space-6);   /* 24px on medium and up      */
  --space-section-gap: var(--space-16);
}

/* Tier 2: semantic component spacing (density-aware, not responsive) */
--space-control-inset-x: var(--space-3);

Common spacing mistakes

Mistake

Off-scale "just this once" values

Each one is harmless; fifty are a second, invisible spacing system. Lint for raw pixel values in spacing properties.

Mistake

Equal spacing everywhere

Using 16px for everything removes the proximity signal. Groups disappear. Vary space deliberately by level.

Mistake

Margins on components

Components that carry their own outer margin collide unpredictably. Let parents own the space between children (CSS gap).

Mistake

Ignoring line-height in vertical spacing

A 16px gap between two text blocks with loose line-heights looks larger than 16px. Align text to the same 4px grid so measured and perceived space match.

Spacing checklist

  • Base unit chosen (4px with an 8px rhythm recommended)
  • Closed scale of ~12–14 values, dense small, sparse large
  • Token names guessable from values
  • Inset / stack / inline vocabulary in specs
  • Proximity rule: within-group < between-group, by 2+ steps
  • Density modes remap tokens; touch targets ≥ 24px (AA), 44–48 on touch
  • Component spacing fixed; layout spacing responsive
  • Lint against raw spacing values

Chapter 10

Grid and layout systems

Grids are how a product decides where things go on every screen size before anyone designs a single screen. In modern products, layout is less about a column grid on a page and more about regions, containers and how they adapt.

Read this if

You are defining breakpoints, designing an app shell or dashboard, or your screens break in different ways on every device.

What you'll leave with
  1. The anatomy of a grid (columns, gutters, margins, containers) and the numbers for each.
  2. A breakpoint system grounded in published systems.
  3. A layout model for SaaS dashboards and complex enterprise applications.

10.1Grid fundamentals

A layout grid divides the available width into columns separated by gutters, inside margins, within a container. Content spans whole columns (and the gutters between them), so edges align across the screen without anyone measuring.

PartDefinitionGuidance
ColumnsVertical divisions content snaps to.4 on phones, 8 on tablets, 12 on desktop is the common pattern.
GuttersFixed space between columns.Use spacing tokens (16–24px). Gutters stay fixed; columns flex.
MarginsSpace between the grid and the screen edge.Grow with screen size: 16px on phones up to 32–80px on large screens.
ContainerThe box the grid lives in; may have a maximum width.Cap reading layouts (~1200–1440px); let data-dense apps go full width.

10.2Breakpoints and responsive grids

Breakpoints are the widths at which the layout changes structure. Set them where your layout needs to change, informed by common device classes, rather than by specific devices, which change every year.

Material 3 window size classes Documented

ClassWidth (dp)
Compact< 600
Medium600–839
Expanded840–1199
Large1200–1599
Extra-large≥ 1600

Source: Material 3 layout guidance.44

IBM Carbon 2x Grid breakpoints Documented

NameFrom (px)Columns
sm3204
md6728
lg105616
xlg131216
max158416

Source: Carbon 2x Grid.45 Carbon's 16-column grid suits dense product UI.

Two mature systems, two different sets of numbers, and both work. The lesson is not to copy either set. Pick a small number of breakpoints (four or five), give them names rather than device labels, and tokenise them so design and code agree. Ledgerly uses Material's classes with 4, 8 and 12 columns.

10.3Fluid, fixed and hybrid layouts

Fluid

Columns stretch with the viewport

Uses all available space. Right for data-dense apps, but long lines of text become unreadable on wide screens.

Fixed

Container has a set width

Predictable, easy to design, but wastes space on large screens and needs separate layouts for small ones.

Hybrid (recommended)

Fluid up to a maximum

Columns flex between breakpoints; the container caps at a maximum width for reading layouts. Apps can opt out of the cap.

Content width

Grids decide where things can go; content width decides how wide reading content should be. Line length for prose is best kept around 45–75 characters,37 which means body text should rarely span all 12 columns of a wide screen. Set content-width tokens independently of the grid:

TokenValueUsed for
layout.width.prose68chArticles, help content, long descriptions
layout.width.form560pxSingle-column forms and settings
layout.width.dialog.md560pxStandard dialogs
layout.width.page1440pxMax container for marketing and reading layouts
layout.width.appnoneData-dense application views, full width

10.4Composing a SaaS dashboard

Most SaaS products are not pages on a grid. They are an app shell (persistent navigation and chrome) around a content region that has its own grid. Defining the shell's regions as part of the system removes a whole category of per-team layout decisions.

Dashboard composition rules

  1. Most important information top-left

    For left-to-right languages, readers scan from the top-left. Put the KPI or chart that answers "is everything OK?" first.

  2. Equal-height rows

    Cards in the same row share a height, so the grid stays visible and the eye can compare them.

  3. Spans from a short list

    Allow 3, 4, 6, 8, 9 and 12 columns on desktop. Avoid 5 and 7, which create misaligned edges.

  4. Mirror for right-to-left

    Use logical properties (inline-start, not left) so Arabic and Hebrew layouts mirror correctly from the same tokens.

10.5Desktop, mobile and alignment

Desktop and mobile are different layouts, not one layout scaled

On mobile, side navigation becomes a bottom bar or a drawer; multi-pane views become single screens with back navigation; tables become lists or cards. Decide these transformations once, as patterns, and every product inherits them.

Align to columns at the page level, to spacing inside components

Page regions and cards align to grid columns. Inside a card, elements align to each other using spacing tokens; a button doesn't need to snap to a column. Trying to grid everything produces rigid, awkward components.

Reflow, and its exceptions

WCAG 2.2 SC 1.4.10 requires content to reflow at a width of 320 CSS px without two-dimensional scrolling, except for content that requires a two-dimensional layout, such as data tables, maps and diagrams.36 Standard Plan the 320px layout of every pattern; scroll horizontally only inside a table, never the whole page.

10.6Layout for complex enterprise applications

Enterprise applications push past the single-grid model. The layout system needs a vocabulary for structures that page grids don't describe:

Multi-pane layouts

List–detail and supporting-pane layouts that show two or three panes side by side on large screens and collapse to one on small. Material documents these as canonical layouts.44

Resizable and collapsible panes

Users of complex tools expect to resize panels. Define minimum and maximum widths as tokens, and remember user preferences.

Nested grids and container queries

A component placed in a narrow pane should adapt to its container, not the viewport. CSS container queries make components responsive to the space they're given.

Sticky regions and dense tables

Sticky headers, frozen first columns and horizontal scrolling inside tables keep context while users work through large datasets.

Layout tokens

"breakpoint": { "medium": "600px", "expanded": "840px", "large": "1200px", "xlarge": "1600px" },
"grid":       { "columns": { "compact": 4, "medium": 8, "expanded": 12 },
                "gutter": "{space.4}", "margin": { "compact": "{space.4}", "expanded": "{space.6}" } },
"layout":     { "sidebar": { "width": "240px", "collapsed": "64px" }, "topbar": { "height": "48px" },
                "width": { "prose": "68ch", "form": "560px", "page": "1440px" } }

A note on breakpoints as tokens: CSS custom properties can't be used inside media query conditions, so breakpoint tokens are compiled to constants (Sass variables, JS constants, or @custom-media where supported) rather than to var().

Grid and layout checklist

  • 4–5 named breakpoints, tokenised for design and code
  • Columns per breakpoint (e.g. 4 / 8 / 12)
  • Gutters and margins from the spacing scale
  • Hybrid container: fluid with a max width for reading
  • Content-width tokens for prose, forms and dialogs
  • App shell regions defined and sized by tokens
  • Mobile transformations defined as patterns
  • Every pattern works at 320px (tables excepted)
  • Logical properties for right-to-left support
  • Container queries for components in panes

Chapter 11

How foundations work together

Colour, type, spacing and layout are not four separate deliverables. They are one system, and the best way to see it is to follow a single component from the first decision to the line of code that ships.

Read this if

You want to see the whole architecture in one place, or you need to explain to engineering how foundations become components.

What you'll leave with
  1. One component traced through five layers: decision, token, component, pattern and production.
  2. A clear picture of what changes, and what doesn't, when a foundation changes.
  3. A foundations readiness checklist to close out Part 02.

11.1One button, five layers

The primary button is the most-used interactive component in most products. Here is every foundation it depends on, and how each one gets from a decision to the screen.

The component, annotated

11.2Into production

The token pipeline compiles the token source into each platform's format. For the web, that's CSS custom properties, which the component consumes. Notice that the component code contains no raw values at all.

/* tokens.css: generated, never hand-edited */
:root {
  --color-brand-700: oklch(0.486 0.172 35);
  --color-brand-800: oklch(0.406 0.146 34);
  --color-action-primary-bg:
    var(--color-brand-700);
  --color-action-primary-bg-hover:
    var(--color-brand-800);
  --space-control-inset-x: var(--space-4);
  --size-control-height: 40px;
}
[data-theme="dark"] {
  --color-action-primary-bg:
    var(--color-brand-400);
}
[data-density="compact"] {
  --size-control-height: 32px;
  --space-control-inset-x: var(--space-2);
}
/* button.css: consumes semantic tokens only */
.button {
  height: var(--size-control-height);
  padding-inline: var(--space-control-inset-x);
  gap: var(--space-2);
  border-radius: var(--radius-control);
  font: var(--type-label-md);
}
.button[data-variant="primary"] {
  background: var(--color-action-primary-bg);
  color: var(--color-action-primary-text);
}
.button[data-variant="primary"]:hover {
  background:
    var(--color-action-primary-bg-hover);
}
.button:focus-visible {
  outline: 2px solid var(--color-focus-ring);
  outline-offset: 2px;
}

Native platforms receive the same tokens as Swift and Kotlin constants from the same source file. The token source is the contract; each platform's components are implementations of it.

11.3When a foundation changes

The real test of the architecture is change. For each kind of change, here is which layers are touched, and how many are not.

ChangePrimitivesSemanticComponentsProductsEffort
Rebrand: new brand hue●○○○Change one seed; ramps regenerate; validate contrast; release.
Add dark theme○●○○One new semantic mapping; validate pairings; release.
Fix secondary-text contrast○●○○One reference change; every product fixed on upgrade.
Add compact density○●◐○Density mapping; check components with fixed internal sizes.
New type scale●◐○◐Values change; products check layouts that depended on old sizes.
White-label for a customer●○○○Generate a brand tier from the customer's seed at runtime or build time.

● changed · ◐ may need review · ○ untouched. These outcomes hold only if components consume semantic tokens exclusively. A single hard-coded hex in a component breaks the chain for that component.

The whole of Part 02 in one sentence

Decide once in OKLCH, on a 4px grid, in a named type scale; encode the decisions as primitive and semantic tokens; let components consume only semantic tokens. Then every future change is a configuration change.

11.4Foundations readiness checklist

Before building components at scale, confirm the foundations are ready. Each item links back to the chapter that explains it.

Colour ch. 07

  • OKLCH ramps on a fixed lightness curve, hex fallbacks generated
  • Semantic colour tokens for bg, surface, border, text, icon, action, feedback, focus
  • Light and dark mappings with every pairing contrast-tested in CI

Typography ch. 08

  • Role-based scale (display, heading, body, label, caption) as composite tokens
  • Line-heights on the 4px grid; tabular numerals available
  • Responsive strategy that respects zoom and text-spacing overrides

Spacing ch. 09

  • 4px-based scale with guessable token names
  • Semantic component spacing with density modes
  • Target sizes meet WCAG 2.2 AA (24px) and platform touch guidance

Layout ch. 10

  • Named breakpoints, columns, gutters and margins as tokens
  • App shell regions and content-width tokens defined
  • Every pattern planned for 320px reflow

Pipeline ch. 06

  • Single token source (DTCG JSON) compiled to all platforms and the design tool
  • Lint rule against raw values in product code

Tokens first, components second.Rule #4 — Layer One

With foundations in place, the next layer is components: their APIs, variants, states and accessibility behaviour. That is where Part 03 of this playbook begins.

About Layer One and the author

Layer One is a design systems studio in Bangalore, India. We set up the foundations, scale them across products and markets, and put in the governance that keeps teams using them.

Aniket Pandey

Aniket leads Layer One. His design systems work spans three very different kinds of organisation:

  • JPMorgan Chase, Senior Designer, Design Systems (2025–present): company-wide design patterns, an AI-assisted workflow for drafting them, and tooling that checks design files and code against the system, used by 500+ designers and 1,000+ engineers.
  • CARS24, Design Systems Lead (2024–25): the design system for 70+ designers and 200+ engineers, a new palette and token architecture for the rebrand, governance, and a pattern library, putting 10+ products in three countries on one token system.
  • IBM, UX Designer, design systems (2021–24): design systems for IBM clients including Cardinal Health and Riyadh Air, from foundations and tokens to governance, contribution and releases.

Source: layerone.co.in.1

The rules we work by

  1. A design system is an agreement, not a library

  2. Audit before you build

  3. Name things so people can guess them

  4. Tokens first, components second

  5. Accessible by default, not by audit

  6. Every decision comes with a reason

  7. Build where the system lives: your files, your repo

  8. Measure time saved, not usage

  9. Docs decide adoption

  10. Leave the team able to run it without us

Where to start

Start with a two-week audit.

We map every style, component and token you have in Figma and code, check accessibility, and give you a ranked plan for what to fix first. Fixed scope, fixed price, and credited in full if you go on to a Foundations build.
